Chapter 21: Capítulo 20

Chapter Notes

This story is written in Spanish and translated into English. If you find any errors, let me know

See the end of the chapter for more notes

 

Mk felt the blood drain from his face.

The garden, which just a second ago had been filled with laughter and cheerful shouts, fell into a deathly silence. The little monkeys froze, tails bristling and eyes wide. Even Macaque, who had been writing without reacting to the game, looked up with a raised eyebrow.

The ink bottle rolled slowly across the table before falling to the ground with a hollow sound. A dark puddle spread over the carefully organized documents, soaking official seals and important scrolls. But worst of all was Sun Wukong’s chest, where a massive black stain stood out against his golden tunic.

Mk swallowed hard.

The king lowered his gaze to his ruined outfit, then to the table… and finally to Mk.

The monarch’s golden eyes gleamed with an unreadable expression. There was no anger on his face, but he wasn’t smiling either.

Panic rose in Mk’s throat. He couldn’t breathe. His mind clouded with memories of the orphanage—of shouting, of punishments, of the cold stare of the director whenever he or another child did something wrong.

What will you do when the differences outweigh the similarities?

The director’s voice seeped into his mind like slow poison, a cruel echo that never fully faded.

And suddenly, he was no longer in the garden.

Cold bit into his skin, his bare feet trembled against the stone floor. In front of him, a caretaker looked at him sternly, rhythmically tapping a cane against his own hand. At his feet, the shattered remains of a vase gleamed under the dim lamp light.

—What happened here?

The question carried an implicit threat—that any answer would be insufficient.

Fear wrapped around him like a familiar shadow. Before his mind could react, his body already had. He lowered his head, shrinking into himself, reducing himself to nothing, preparing for the scolding, for the punishment… for whatever was to come.

But the blow never came.

Instead, a different sound broke the silence.

—Pffft—!

Was that… laughter?

Mk cautiously lifted his gaze.

Sun Wukong’s shoulders were shaking… and suddenly, he burst out laughing.

—HAHAHAHA! Oh, no way! —The monarch held his forehead with one hand, laughing uncontrollably—. Did you see that, Plum? HAHAHA!

Macaque, who had initially kept his usual impassive expression, let out a mocking smile.

—Well, take it as a sign to change things up from all the gold and yellow.—he commented, pointing at the stain on the tunic.

Wukong leaned back in his chair with a hand on his chest, still laughing.

—And right when I was inspired with my speech! Mk, nice aim! HAHAHAHA!

Mk blinked, unsure if this was a joke or if Wukong truly wasn’t mad. The little monkeys, seeing their king laugh, began shrieking with laughter as well, rolling across the grass in pure delight.

The cub didn’t know what to do. A part of him still expected someone to tell him he was in trouble at any moment. But when Wukong flashed him a beaming smile, something in his chest loosened.

Shortly after, the servants cleared the table of documents and began preparing it for the meal.

—Wukong, put something on already! —Macaque exclaimed, pinching the bridge of his nose in an attempt to keep his patience.

The king had removed the stained top of his outfit, left only in his pants with his chest bare. He was busy tossing the little monkeys into the air and catching them in chaotic play.

—Bah! Relax a little, Plum, it’s hot —he said shamelessly, not stopping his game.

—That’s not the reason!

—Then what is it? —Wukong stopped what he was doing and turned to him with a mischievous grin—. I thought you liked what you saw.

The Monkey King placed his hands on his hips strategically, giving Macaque a clear view of his torso.

Macaque’s six ears instantly turned red.

—WUKONG!

The little monkeys giggled conspiratorially as Sun Wukong laughed heartily, his laughter rumbling through the garden like playful thunder. It wasn’t the cruel taunt Mk knew, but a laughter full of genuine joy, of satisfaction from a well-executed prank.

Mk watched them in silence, with a mix of curiosity and bewilderment. They seemed so… happy together. They pushed each other, played tricks, stole things only to return them seconds later with laughter. There was no malice in their games, just affection disguised as mischief.

The feeling of relief still weighed on his chest. He still didn’t fully understand why no one was angry. At the orphanage, an accident like that would have been unforgivable. He would have been punished, sent to the mines… or worse. The sound of bamboo canes striking echoed in his memory like a distant ghost.

Instinctively, he rubbed his right shoulder, as if the pain of old wounds could awaken just from remembering them.

But his relief didn’t fully erase the fear. Wukong and Macaque were not harmless. They could hurt. He had seen it with his own eyes. The memory of the king’s hands, covered in blood after what he did to the orphanage caretaker, flashed through his mind like lightning. A shiver ran down his spine.

—Mk!

The voice pulled him abruptly from his thoughts. He blinked, disoriented.

—The food is ready!

He turned and saw Macaque motioning to him from the table, where steaming dishes now awaited. Mk took a deep breath, pushing the memories away.

He stood up and approached the table with hesitant steps. He still felt the need to apologize. Even though the Monkey King had laughed and dismissed the ink incident, something inside him kept screaming that he had done something wrong. A commoner should not stain the clothes of a king.

As always, Wukong and Macaque sat together, sharing the same space with the ease of those who had remained side by side for centuries. Beside them, a chair had been placed for him. It was the fourth time he sat at the table with them, and yet, the feeling of strangeness never faded.

The plate before him contained a simple salad with fresh, crisp vegetables. Nothing extravagant. Nothing unfamiliar. A relief. He was used to eating scraps, wilted vegetables pulled from a restaurant’s trash, so this was relatively closer to his normal.

With some clumsiness, he struggled with the utensils until he managed to eat with relative normality.

—He should eat more meat —Wukong commented, watching him out of the corner of his eye while biting into a peach.

—You heard our brother —Macaque replied without even looking up from his plate—. Not until his stomach gets used to it. It was already irresponsible of us to give him so many sweets this morning. His body could have rejected it.

—Okay, okay —the Monkey King murmured before turning his attention to Mk—. Do you like the food, cub?

Mk nodded, still chewing.

There was a brief silence in which he lowered his gaze, his fingers tightening around the edge of his plate. The unease still lingered in his chest, growing.

—Monkey King… —His voice was smaller than he wanted—. I wanted to apologize for the ink. I didn’t mean to spill it.

Wukong raised an eyebrow, chewing leisurely.

—Mmm? That? It’s not a big deal, kid.

—YES, IT IS!

The shout escaped before he could stop it.

The silence that fell over the table was heavy. Macaque put his chopsticks down on the plate, and Wukong paused with the fruit halfway to his mouth, both of them staring at him in surprise.

Mk felt embarrassment rising in his throat like bile. He lowered his head, clenching his fists on his lap.

—It’s just… I… —The words got stuck in his throat, smothered by a fear that never truly went away.

Mk lowered his gaze to the plate, clenching his fists over his lap. His heart pounded in his chest, and shame burned his throat.

—I… I shouldn’t have been so careless… —he murmured, but his voice was barely a whisper.

Beside him, Macaque and Wukong exchanged a fleeting glance.

—Kid… —the Monkey King started in a softer tone.

But Mk didn’t let him finish.

—If a peasant dirtied a king’s clothes, they should be punished. I… —he swallowed, his mind drifting back to a past he didn’t want to remember—. I don’t want you to think I don’t respect you…

The words hung in the air. An invisible weight settled over the table.

Wukong studied him carefully. Something about the rigidity of his shoulders, the way he avoided his gaze, reminded him of a cornered animal. He sighed, resting an elbow on the table as he leaned slightly toward the boy.

—Mk, listen —he said calmly—. It was an accident. I assure you, I’m not angry. The place you come from has taught you that respect only comes through fear and pain. I want you to know that those people don’t deserve your respect. They were horrible beings who will get what they deserve.

—This isn’t the orphanage, nor any other place where you have to walk in fear. There are no punishments for accidents here.

Mk looked up cautiously, meeting the king’s golden eyes—warm and firm.

—Alright?

The cub hesitated but eventually nodded.

—Alright…

He still wasn’t sure if he could believe those words. But, for the first time in a long while, he wanted to.

Wukong watched him in silence, his golden gaze analyzing every little gesture the cub made. Finally, he exchanged a meaningful look with Macaque before speaking.

—At the orphanage… were you punished for things like this?

Mk shifted in his seat, uncomfortable.

—Sometimes.

His voice was low, almost indifferent, but the tension in his shoulders betrayed him.

—When something broke, or when a task wasn’t completed… —He continued, as if reciting a simple fact, but his tone was distant, empty—. Once, we were punished because leaks had formed in the roof. By the time we noticed, the floor was already soaked. It was our fault for not seeing it sooner…

Silence.

Wukong swallowed, his jaw tightening.

—I see… And… —his voice wavered for just an instant before hardening with forced control—. How were you usually punished?

Mk averted his gaze, his throat closing up.

He didn’t want to answer.

Not because he couldn’t… but because he didn’t know how to explain something that had always been a rule, something he had never questioned until now.

Macaque was the one who broke the tension, his tone softer than usual.

—You don’t have to answer now if you don’t want to, Mk.

The cub looked up.

—But I want you to know that we’ll always be here if you ever decide to tell us.

Mk didn’t want to keep talking. Every word seemed to open wounds he had learned to ignore. But at the same time, he felt like he owed it to the rulers.

He took a deep breath.

—Cursed children… were taken to the mines.

The words fell heavy into the silence.

Wukong leaned forward, his gaze sharpening with renewed interest.

—You mean the mines beneath the orphanage?

Mk nodded slowly.

—Yes… —his voice was barely a murmur, but each syllable was steeped in dark memories—. When you make a mistake too big… you bring chaos into the world. To purge it… you need to work very hard in the mines, searching for order.

Macaque narrowed his eyes.

—What were you searching for? What were you supposed to find?

Mk opened his mouth… but no answer came.

—I… —they never explained anything. They only obeyed.—. I don’t know…

He didn’t know what they were looking for down there. He only remembered seeing the darkness from the doorway, the cold seeping into his bones, the weight of the stone, and the sound of pickaxes striking the walls.

And the fear.

Always the fear.

He hadn’t realized he was trembling until he felt a firm, warm hand rest on his shoulder.

—Hey, easy. Everything’s going to be okay.

Wukong’s voice was gentle but filled with unwavering certainty. Before he could react, the king lifted him effortlessly from his chair and wrapped him in a warm embrace. Mk tensed instinctively, but the monarch’s warmth and his scent—of sky and sun—felt strangely comforting.

—Lady Bones Demon… that demon who ran the orphanage —Wukong’s voice turned graver, laced with restrained fury—. She’s insane. Everything she told you was a lie. She only used you to make you work for her.

His words were firm, filled with conviction. A promise made of steel and fire.

Wukong ran his palm over Mk’s cheek with unexpected tenderness.

—She is a despicable, power-hungry being —he whispered—. And I swear, by my kingdom and my name, that no cub is responsible for this world’s chaos just for making innocent mistakes.

Mk lifted his gaze, meeting the king’s golden eyes. There was no mockery or condescension in them. Only truth.

The entire garden seemed to hold its breath. Even the birds had fallen silent.

Mk lowered his gaze, looking at Wukong’s hand still resting on his cheek. He didn’t know if he could believe those words…

He could feel how the rulers had changed their demeanor. They were contemplative, their gazes lost in some distant point, immersed in dark thoughts. But Wukong didn’t seem to want to let him go.

Carefully, Mk let himself lean against the king’s chest, seeking refuge in his warmth, letting the heat of his arms calm the tremors still coursing through his body.

And so they stayed. In silence. For a long time.

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

Mk sintió cómo la sangre le abandonaba el rostro.  

 

El jardín, que hasta hace un segundo estaba lleno de risas y gritos alegres, quedó sumido en un silencio sepulcral. Los pequeños monos se quedaron quietos, con las colas erizadas y los ojos muy abiertos. Incluso Macaque, que había estado escribiendo sin inmutarse ante el juego, levantó la vista con una ceja arqueada.  

 

El bote de tinta rodó lentamente sobre la mesa antes de caer al suelo con un sonido hueco. Un charco oscuro se extendía sobre los documentos cuidadosamente organizados, empapando sellos oficiales y pergaminos importantes. Pero lo peor de todo era el pecho de Sun Wukong, donde una enorme mancha negra destacaba sobre su túnica dorada.  

 

Mk tragó saliva con fuerza.  

 

El rey bajó la mirada a su traje arruinado, luego a la mesa… y finalmente a Mk.  

 

Los ojos dorados del monarca brillaban con una expresión ilegible. No había ira en su rostro, pero tampoco sonreía.  

 

Mk sintió el pánico subirle por la garganta. No podía respirar. Su mente se nubló con recuerdos del orfanato, de gritos, de castigos, de la fría mirada de la directora cuando él o algún otro niño hacía algo mal.  

 

¿Qué harás cuando las diferencias pesen más que las similitudes?

 

La voz de la directora se filtró en su mente como un veneno lento, un eco cruel que nunca terminaba de desvanecerse.  

 

Y, de repente, ya no estaba en el jardín.  

 

El frío le mordía la piel, sus pies descalzos temblaban sobre el suelo de piedra. Frente a él, un cuidador lo miraba con severidad, golpeando rítmicamente una vara contra su propia mano. A sus pies, los restos de un jarrón roto brillaban bajo la tenue luz de la lámpara.  

 

—¿Qué pasó aquí? —La pregunta llegó con la amenaza implícita de que cualquier respuesta sería insuficiente.  

 

El miedo lo envolvió como una sombra familiar. Antes de que su mente pudiera reaccionar, su cuerpo ya lo había hecho. Bajó la cabeza, encogiéndose sobre sí mismo, reduciéndose a la nada, preparándose para el regaño, para el castigo… para lo que fuera que viniera.

 

Pero el golpe nunca llegó.  

 

En su lugar, un sonido distinto rompió el silencio.  

 

—¡Pffft—!  

 

Era… ¿una risa?  

 

Mk alzó la vista con cautela.  

 

Sun Wukong tenía los hombros temblando… y de repente soltó una carcajada.  

 

—¡JAJAJAJAJA! ¡Ay, no puede ser! —El monarca se sujetó la frente con una mano mientras se reía sin control—. ¿Viste eso, Ciruela? ¡JAJAJA!  

 

Macaque, que al principio había mantenido su expresión impasible, dejó escapar una sonrisa burlona.  

 

—Bueno, tomalo como una señal para variar un poco del dorado y amarillo.—comentó, señalando la mancha en su túnica.  

 

Wukong se inclinó hacia atrás en la silla con una mano en el pecho, todavía riendo.  

 

—¡Y justo cuando estaba inspirado en mi discurso! Mk, ¡Buena puntería! JAJAJAJAJAJA.

 

Mk parpadeó, sin saber si aquello era una broma o si Wukong realmente no estaba molesto. Los pequeños monos, al ver que su rey se reía, comenzaron a chillar de risa también, rodando por el césped de pura diversión.  

 

El cachorro no supo qué hacer. Una parte de él aún esperaba que en cualquier momento alguien le dijera que estaba en problemas. Pero cuando Wukong le dedicó una sonrisa radiante, sintió que algo en su pecho se aflojaba.  

 

Poco después, los sirvientes despejaron la mesa de documentos y comenzaron a prepararla para la comida.

 

—¡Wukong, tápate de una vez! —exclamó Macaque, llevándose los dedos al puente de la nariz en un intento por no perder la paciencia.

 

El rey se había quitado la parte superior manchada de su atuendo, quedando solo con los pantalones y el pecho descubierto. Estaba entretenido lanzando a los pequeños monos al aire y atrapándolos en un juego caótico.

 

—¡Bah! Relájate un poco, Ciruela, hace calor —dijo con descaro, sin dejar de jugar.

 

—¡No es por eso!

 

—¿Entonces por qué es? —Wukong detuvo lo que estaba haciendo y giró para mirarlo con una sonrisa pícara—. Creí que te gustaba lo que veías.

 

El Rey Mono apoyó las manos en sus caderas estratégicamente, dándole a Macaque una vista clara de su torso.

 

Las seis orejas de Macaque se tiñeron de rojo al instante.

 

—¡WUKONG!

 

Los pequeños monos soltaron risitas cómplices mientras Sun Wukong se reía a carcajadas, su risa retumbando por el jardín como un trueno juguetón. No era la burla cruel que Mk conocía, sino una risa llena de alegría genuina, de satisfacción por una travesura bien hecha.  

 

Mk los observó en silencio, con una mezcla de curiosidad y desconcierto. Parecían tan… felices juntos. Se empujaban, se hacían bromas, se robaban cosas solo para devolvérselas segundos después entre risas. No había malicia en sus juegos, solo cariño disfrazado de travesura.  

 

 

La sensación de alivio seguía pesando en su pecho. Aún no entendía del todo por qué nadie estaba enojado. En el orfanato, un accidente como aquel habría sido imperdonable. Lo habrían castigado, enviado a las minas… o algo peor. El sonido de los golpes con palos de bambú resonó en su memoria como un eco distante.  

 

Instintivamente, se frotó el hombro derecho, como si el dolor de antiguas heridas pudiera despertar solo por recordarlas.  

 

Pero su alivio no apagó del todo el temor. Wukong y Macaque no eran inofensivos. Podían herir. Lo había visto con sus propios ojos. El recuerdo de las manos del rey, cubiertas de sangre después de lo que le hizo al cuidador del orfanato, le atravesó la mente como un relámpago. Un escalofrío le recorrió la espalda.  

 

—¡Mk!  

 

La voz lo sacó de golpe de sus pensamientos. Parpadeó, desorientado.  

 

—¡Ya está la comida!  

 

Se giró y vio a Macaque haciéndole un gesto desde la mesa, donde ahora había platos humeantes esperándolos. Mk respiró hondo, alejando los recuerdos.

 

Se puso de pie y se acercó a la mesa con pasos inseguros. Aún sentía la necesidad de disculparse. Aunque el Rey Mono había reído y restado importancia al incidente con la tinta, algo dentro de él seguía gritando que había cometido una falta. Un plebeyo no debería ensuciar las ropas de un rey.  

 

Como siempre, Wukong y Macaque se habían sentado juntos, compartiendo el mismo espacio con la naturalidad de quienes han permanecido unidos por siglos. A su lado, una silla había sido colocada para él. Era la cuarta vez que se sentaba a la mesa con ellos y, aun así, la sensación de extrañeza no desaparecía.  

 

El plato frente a él contenía una ensalada sencilla, con vegetales frescos y crujientes. Nada extravagante. Nada desconocido. Un alivio. Estaba acostumbrado a comer sobras, verduras marchitas sacadas de la basura de algún restaurante así que esto relativamente más cercano a su día a día.

 

Con algo de torpeza, luchó con los utensilios hasta que logró llevárselos a la boca con relativa normalidad.  

 

—Debería comer más carne —comentó Wukong, observándolo de reojo mientras mordía un melocotón.  

 

—Ya escuchaste a nuestro hermano —respondió Macaque sin siquiera levantar la vista de su plato—. No hasta que su estómago se acostumbre. Ya fue bastante irresponsable de nuestra parte darle tanto dulce esta mañana. Su cuerpo podría haberlo rechazado.  

 

—Okey, okey —murmuró el Rey Mono antes de volver su atención a Mk—. ¿Te gusta la comida, cachorro?  

 

Mk asintió, aún con la boca llena.  

 

Hubo un breve silencio en el que él bajó la mirada, sus dedos apretándose alrededor del borde del plato. La inquietud seguía ahí, creciendo en su pecho.  

 

—Rey Mono… —Su voz sonó más pequeña de lo que quería—. Quería pedirte perdón por lo de la tinta. No era mi intención derramarla.  

 

Wukong arqueó una ceja, masticando con tranquilidad.  

 

—¿Mmm? ¿Eso? No tiene importancia, pequeño.  

 

—¡SÍ LA TIENE!  

 

El grito escapó antes de que pudiera detenerlo.  

 

El silencio cayó sobre la mesa como una losa. Macaque dejó sus palillos sobre el plato y Wukong se quedó con la fruta a medio camino de su boca, ambos observándolo con sorpresa.  

 

Mk sintió la vergüenza subiéndole por la garganta como bilis. Bajó la cabeza, apretando los puños sobre sus piernas.  

 

—Es que… yo… —Las palabras se le atoraron en la garganta, sofocadas por un miedo que nunca desaparecía del todo. 

 

Mk bajó la mirada al plato, apretando los puños sobre su regazo. Sentía el corazón martillando en su pecho, la vergüenza quemándole la garganta.  

 

—Yo… no debí ser tan descuidado… —murmuró, pero su voz apenas fue un susurro.  

 

A su lado, Macaque y Wukong intercambiaron una mirada fugaz.  

 

—Pequeño… —comenzó el Rey Mono con un tono más suave.  

 

Pero Mk no le dejó terminar.  

 

—Si un plebeyo ensuciara la ropa de un rey, debería recibir un castigo. Yo… —tragó saliva, su mente regresando a un pasado que no quería recordar—. No quiero que penséis que no os respeto…  

 

Las palabras quedaron flotando en el aire. Un peso invisible se asentó en la mesa.  

 

Wukong lo observó con detenimiento. Algo en la rigidez de sus hombros, en la manera en que evitaba su mirada, le recordó a un animal acorralado. Suspiró y apoyó un codo en la mesa, inclinándose levemente hacia el niño.  

 

—Mk, escucha —dijo con calma— Fue un accidente, te aseguro de que no estoy enfadado. El lugar de donde vienes te ha enseñado solo el respeto a través del miedo y el dolor. Quiero que sepas que esas personas no merecen tu respeto. Eran seres horribles que recibirán su merecido.

 

—Aquí no estamos en el orfanato, ni en ningún otro sitio donde tengas que caminar con miedo. Aquí no hay castigos por accidentes.  

 

Mk levantó la vista con cautela, encontrándose con los ojos dorados del monarca, cálidos y firmes.  

 

—¿De acuerdo?  

 

El cachorro dudó, pero finalmente asintió.  

 

—De acuerdo…  

 

Aún no estaba seguro de poder creer en aquellas palabras. Pero, por primera vez en mucho tiempo, quiso hacerlo.  

 

Wukong lo observó en silencio, su mirada dorada analizando cada pequeño gesto del cachorro. Finalmente, intercambió una mirada significativa con Macaque antes de hablar.  

 

—En el orfanato… ¿os castigaban por este tipo de cosas?  

 

Mk se removió en su asiento, incómodo.  

 

—A veces.  

 

Su voz sonó baja, casi indiferente, pero la tensión en sus hombros lo delataba.  

 

—Cuando se rompía algo o alguna tarea quedaba sin hacer… —Continuó, como si estuviera recitando un hecho cualquiera, pero su tono era distante, vacío—. Una vez nos castigaron porque se habían formado goteras en el techo. Cuando nos dimos cuenta, el suelo ya estaba empapado. Fue nuestra culpa por no haberlo visto antes…  

 

Silencio.  

 

Wukong tragó saliva, su mandíbula tensándose.  

 

—Entiendo… Y… —Su voz vaciló apenas un instante antes de endurecerse con un control forzado—. ¿Cómo os castigaban normalmente?  

 

Mk apartó la mirada, su garganta se cerró de golpe.  

 

No quería responder.  

 

No porque no pudiera… sino porque no sabía cómo explicar algo que siempre había sido una norma, algo que nunca había cuestionado hasta ahora.  

 

Macaque fue quien rompió la tensión, su tono más suave de lo habitual.  

 

—No tienes que responder ahora si no quieres, Mk.  

 

El cachorro alzó la vista.  

 

—Pero quiero que sepas que siempre estaremos aquí si algún día decides contarnos.  

 

Mk no quería seguir hablando. Cada palabra parecía abrir heridas que había aprendido a ignorar. Pero, al mismo tiempo, sentía que se lo debía a los gobernantes.  

 

Respiró hondo.  

 

—A los niños malditos… se los llevaban a las minas.  

 

Las palabras cayeron pesadas en el silencio.  

 

Wukong se inclinó hacia adelante, su mirada afilándose con renovado interés.  

 

—¿Te refieres a las minas debajo del orfanato?  

 

Mk asintió lentamente.  

 

—Sí… —su voz era apenas un murmullo, pero cada sílaba estaba impregnada de recuerdos sombríos—. Cuando cometes un error demasiado grande… traes el caos al mundo. Para purgarlo… necesitas trabajar muy duro en las minas, buscando el orden.  

 

Macaque entrecerró los ojos.  

 

—¿Qué buscaban? ¿Qué tenías que encontrar?  

 

Mk abrió la boca… pero ninguna respuesta llegó.  

 

—Yo… —nunca les explicaban nada. Ellos solo obedecían.—. No lo sé…  

 

No sabía qué era lo que buscaban allí abajo. Solo recordaba ver desde la puerta la oscuridad, el frío que se metía en los huesos, el peso de la piedra y el sonido de los picos golpeando contra las paredes.  

 

Y el miedo.  

 

Siempre el miedo.

 

No se había dado cuenta de que estaba temblando hasta que sintió una mano firme y cálida posarse en su hombro.  

 

—Hey, tranquilo. Todo va a estar bien.  

 

La voz de Wukong era suave, pero cargada de una certeza inquebrantable. Antes de que pudiera reaccionar, el rey lo levantó con facilidad de su silla y lo envolvió en un abrazo cálido. Mk se tensó por instinto, pero el calor del monarca y su aroma a cielo y sol le resultaban extrañamente reconfortantes.  

 

—Lady Bones Demon… ese demonio que dirigía el orfanato —la voz de Wukong se tornó más grave, con un matiz de ira contenida—. Está loca. Todo lo que os dijo es mentira. Solo os utilizaba para que trabajarais para ella.  

 

Sus palabras eran firmes, llenas de convicción. Una promesa hecha de acero y fuego.  

 

Wukong deslizó su palma por la mejilla de Mk con una ternura inesperada.  

 

—Es un ser despreciable y sediento de poder —susurró—. Y te juro, por mi reino y mi nombre, que ningún cachorro es responsable del caos de este mundo por cometer errores inocentes.  

 

Mk alzó la mirada, encontrándose con los ojos dorados del rey. No había burla ni condescendencia en ellos. Solo verdad.  

 

El jardín entero pareció contener la respiración. Hasta los pájaros habían enmudecido.  

 

Mk bajó la vista, observando la mano de Wukong que aún descansaba sobre su mejilla. No sabía si podía creer en esas palabras… 

 

Sintió cómo los gobernantes habían cambiado su actitud. Estaban meditativos, su mirada perdida en algún punto lejano, sumidos en pensamientos oscuros. Pero Wukong no parecía querer soltarlo.  

 

Con cuidado, Mk dejó caer su cuerpo contra el torso del rey, buscando refugio en su calor, dejando que la calidez de sus brazos calmara los temblores que aún recorrían su cuerpo.  

 

Así se quedaron. En silencio. Durante un largo tiempo.

I’m being plagiarized. Or rather, my work is being stolen. And I don’t mean people who’ve been inspired by this AU to create their own “royalty” stories with the LMK characters. In fact, I love that what I write can inspire others; it fills me with pride and joy.

Thank you for reading this far. Now, please enjoy the chapter!

 

 

 

Mk was starting to get fed up with people.  

 

It wasn’t that he didn’t appreciate the care he was receiving—of course not. His body was stronger, his wounds were healing quickly, and for the first time in his life, his stomach was full every single day. In just five days at the palace, he had gained weight and regained some color in his face. But that sense of physical well-being couldn’t silence the whirlwind of thoughts eating away at him from the inside.  

 

His life had fallen into a kind of routine. In the mornings, right after breakfast, his bandages were changed and his wounds checked. Then, the rulers met with their advisors to go over kingdom matters. If there were public audiences, he was left with Mr. Tang, always under the watchful eyes of the guards. At midday, they usually ate in the garden, surrounded by little monkeys who cheerfully squealed as they stole food whenever someone let their guard down.  

 

The afternoons were reserved for exploration and games. The rulers would take him walking through the mountains, showing him beautiful landscapes he never could have imagined. Sometimes they played with the small primates, who insisted on putting them on different teams—because together, they were nearly unbeatable. Wukong and Macaque didn’t seem to mind the competition between them; in fact, they enjoyed it, with challenging smiles and looks full of camaraderie.

 

Lately, Macaque had been teaching him how to play Mahjong. The warrior seemed to enjoy it in a special way, as if playing with Mk held a deeper meaning for him. Mk, for his part, found in the tiles and the strategy a distraction that helped him forget—even if only for a moment—the weight of his new life.  

 

But the constant attention was suffocating.  

 

There was always someone around: guards with unreadable expressions, servants who tended to any need before he even voiced it, and above all, the rulers, who seemed unwilling to leave his side. Wherever he turned his head, they were there. Watching over him. Watching him.  

 

It was… too much.  

 

The only times he was left with Mr. Tang—and a small army of guards stationed in the shadows—were when Wukong and Macaque attended court audiences. But even then, the feeling of being watched never left him.  

 

It was suffocating.  

 

He was used to solitude, to silence, to losing himself in his own thoughts without interruptions. Now, he couldn’t take a single step without someone close behind.  

 

He needed a break. Just five minutes. No concerned voices. No watchful eyes.  

 

He could take care of himself, for heaven’s sake. He’d been doing it his whole life.

 

 

It was a sunny morning, and the rulers had once again left him with Mr. Tang while they attended a meeting about border affairs. The monk, as usual, was lost in his world of ink and scrolls, writing with a meticulous calm that sharply contrasted with the impatience growing inside Mk.  

 

This was his chance.  

 

He carefully set the colored pencils down on the table and stood up with an air of calm.  

 

—I'm going to the bathroom —he announced, not looking directly at the monk.  

 

—All right —Tang replied without lifting his gaze, his voice calm, distracted.  

 

Mk left the library with a façade of tranquility, immediately sensing the silent presence of the two guards who, like disciplined shadows, followed a few steps behind.  

 

He couldn’t rush. He had to seem casual. Harmless.  

 

His eyes landed on the curve in the hallway just a few meters ahead. He knew exactly what he had to do: he had already memorized that corner, rehearsed every move in his mind. He just needed to get there.  

 

He picked up the pace just slightly—enough not to raise suspicion. He glanced over his shoulder. The guards were keeping their distance. Perfect.  

 

Five steps.  

 

Four.  

 

Three.  

 

His tail tensed with anticipation, as if it too knew the time had come.  

 

He turned the corner and, in a single motion, jumped onto a small decorative table set against the wall. Using the momentum, he launched himself upward, grabbing hold with hands and feet onto the large banner proudly hanging from the ceiling, emblazoned with the kingdom's symbol. He climbed swiftly, the banner swaying slightly under his weight. In seconds, he had scrambled up to the wooden beams crossing the ceiling, where he hid among the shadows, holding his breath.  

 

From his hiding spot, he watched as the two guards turned the corner… and froze.  

 

—Where is he? —one of them whispered, already starting to panic.  

 

—Did you see him turn here!? —asked the other, eyes wide, scanning the area.

 

A second later, both of them ran off in opposite directions, calling out his name.

Mk finally let out the breath he’d been holding and allowed himself a proud smile.

Victory.

With a precise leap, he reached the next beam in the hallway, then the next... and another one. He moved as if the air itself carried him, with a lightness only someone who had learned to survive in the tightest spaces could possess. In the blink of an eye, he spotted an open window and slipped outside.

The fresh air hit his face with a mix of freedom and adrenaline. He ran along the packed dirt paths surrounding the castle, his heart pounding and a wild smile tugging at his lips. The wind ruffled his fur as his feet moved deftly down a path he knew well.

He finally arrived at a lush tree, with thick and sturdy branches, rising atop a quiet hill at the edge of the eastern garden. He had seen it before from a distance, memorizing each branch like a secret map. He climbed it with ease, his claws gripping the bark, and within seconds, he was nestled in one of the highest branches.

With a long, satisfied groan, he stretched like a cat in the sun, letting his body finally rest. He closed his eyes and allowed himself to be wrapped in the murmur of wind-blown leaves, in the gentle warmth of sunlight filtering through the canopy.

He sighed in relief. Finally. Finally, a moment alone. No voices, no hands trying to help, no eyes watching him.

The constant attention of the last few days was driving him mad. He appreciated the care, of course, but he wasn’t used to it. He had spent so long hiding from the world that now, being seen every second felt like living under a magnifying glass. This —this high, hidden, silent place— was exactly what he needed.

He’d go back before anyone truly worried about his absence. In time for lunch, with renewed energy.

He opened his eyes and scanned the horizon. From up there, he had an enviable view of the mountain. He could see the outer paths weaving through trees and terraces, the glinting points of armor on soldiers patrolling the trails, the majestic curve of the castle hugging the cliffside.

And then his gaze dropped.

There, at the foot of the mountain, built into the base of the castle, he spotted a heavy iron door set into the rock. Three pairs of warriors stood guard, firm, with drawn swords gleaming in the sun like silent warnings.

 

They had to be the dungeons.

Mk tilted his head in curiosity, ears swiveling attentively. Six guards watching over a single door. That was a lot—even for palace dungeons.

One of the soldiers stepped forward, gripped the thick iron handle, and turned it with effort. The screech that echoed from the door as it opened was so sharp and piercing it reached all the way to the treetop where Mk was perched, making him wince and pin his ears back in discomfort.

Beyond the threshold, there was nothing to see. Just a thick, almost living blackness that seemed to devour the light trying to sneak in. A staircase led down into the depths of the mountain, swallowed by a darkness that had no end. The guard descended without hesitation, vanishing into the shadows, and a few seconds later, the door slammed shut behind him with a muffled boom that echoed even from that distance.

Mk leaned forward, resting his elbows on his knees, intrigued. Since his life had become filled with calm and comfort, something new had begun to grow inside him: a spark of curiosity, almost reckless.

What could be down there? Were they as deep as the mines beneath the orphanage? Deeper even?

The thought sent a chill down his spine. His expression hardened and he leaned back slightly on the branch, crossing his arms. No. Better not. Some doors weren't meant to be opened—not even with your eyes.

That’s when something else caught his attention.

From his perch, he could see part of the castle’s interior through the wide windows and balconies. And what he saw made his whole body tense. Patrols of soldiers were rushing from one end of the hallways to the other, streaks of color darting through the corridors. He could hear shouting—short, urgent commands barked across the space. Some of the guards poured out into the grounds, armed, forming ranks beneath the golden banners of the realm.

Mk straightened on the branch, uneasy. His tail twitched nervously behind him.

—What... what’s going on? —he murmured to himself.

An attack? No, that was impossible. No one in their right mind would dare to attack the rulers of the realm, especially not on their own mountain. But the frenzied movement was real. You could feel the tension in the air, like electricity prickling at your skin.

The cub swallowed hard, feeling a tight pressure start to build in his chest. He no longer felt safe among the branches. It wasn’t exciting anymore.

He decided it was best to go back. The sooner, the better.

Mk climbed down the tree with the same instinctive agility he’d used to get up minutes before. His paws slid between branches and leaves as if they were part of his own body, like he belonged to that high place. Every movement flowed with the precision of someone who had spent their whole life running, hiding, surviving.

When his feet touched the ground, his breath steadied, and a flicker of pride crossed his face. He straightened with a hop, brushed the leaves off his tunic, and took off running along the dirt path skirting the outer walls of the castle.

But he didn’t get far.

The forest shadows stirred. It was so subtle at first he barely noticed—a shift in the density of the air, a whisper among the trees. Then, everything happened in a second.

The shadows cast on the ground began to move. They slithered like spilled ink, alive and aware, crawling across the earth toward him.

Mk barely managed to take a step back before a wave of darkness cut off his path. He stumbled in surprise and hit the ground hard. He scrambled upright, breath ragged, heart pounding in his ears.

In front of him, the shadows rose.

They took shape slowly, like smoke condensing and solidifying. Two glowing eyes emerged from the center of the mist, full of fury and anxiety. The figure completed itself in a matter of seconds.

The warrior let the shadows slide off his body like spilled water, flowing down in dark waves until they formed a more human, more tangible silhouette. His shadow returned to its rightful place beneath his feet, as if nothing had happened. But everything about him radiated barely restrained fury.

There he stood—tall and imposing, shoulders tense, fists clenched, brow furrowed in an expression that brooked no excuses.

Mk opened his mouth to speak, but didn’t get the chance.

—Mk! —Macaque’s voice cracked like thunder as he closed the distance in a blink— What the hell are you doing out here!? Why are you alone!?

The cub took a step back, but not fast enough. Macaque’s hands were already gripping his shoulders. Not roughly, but with an intensity that knocked the air from his lungs. The ruler’s eyes—normally calm like a still, dark lake—now burned with a storm of emotion: worry, anger, panic.

—You can’t just disappear like that! —his voice trembled, not from weakness, but from the strain of having held fear back for too long— We’ve been looking for you everywhere! We thought you’d been...! —he stopped, swallowing hard.

Mk stood frozen, unable to speak. His heart pounded so hard it hurt.

—B-but... —he stammered, confused— I haven’t been gone more than... thirty minutes?

—Never leave without permission again —Macaque cut in firmly. His gaze was hard, immovable, filled with an intensity that left no room for protest— Do you hear me?

Mk nodded silently, feeling the warrior’s words carve deep into his chest.

Macaque closed his eyes for a second, as if he needed to pull himself together. Then, without warning, he pulled Mk into a hug. One of those hugs that wrapped around more than just your body—they wrapped around your soul.

Mk stayed stiff at first. But then, slowly, he let his hands grip the fabric of the ruler’s tunic. He felt his eyes fill with tears—hot, inevitable, heavy with guilt, fear... and something else. An old, poorly buried pain.

When Macaque led him back into the castle, he did so in silence. He didn’t let go of his hand for even a moment.

Mk kept his head down, steps small and reserved. He didn’t say a word. He knew he had caused trouble. That he had angered the rulers. And for the first time, that hurt more than he expected.

Mk kept his head down, steps small, almost timid. He didn’t dare say a word. He felt the weight of silence heavier than any shout. He knew he had caused a problem. He had worried the rulers. But what hurt most was that sharp feeling in his chest: he didn’t want to have disappointed them.

—You’re grounded —Macaque said suddenly, his voice dry as a whip crack.

Mk looked up, surprised. He stared with wide eyes, but the warrior didn’t look back. He kept walking, serious, steady, eyes fixed ahead.

—No more mountain walks for a while.

Mk felt something tighten inside him.

They crossed the castle’s threshold. The doors closed behind them with a heavy, muffled boom, followed by the unmistakable sound of a lock sliding into place. A metallic echo that sealed more than just an entrance.

 

 

Antes de comenzar el capítulo, me gustaría informar de algo importante. Normalmente no me gusta dejar este tipo de comentarios dentro del propio texto, pero creo que esta vez es necesario.

 

Estoy siendo plagiada. O, mejor dicho, me están robando el trabajo. Y no me refiero a personas que se han inspirado en este AU para crear su propia historia de "realeza" con los personajes de LMK. De hecho, me encanta que lo que escribo pueda inspirar a otros; me llena de orgullo y alegría.

 

No, me refiero a un caso de copia y pega literal de, hasta ahora, los dos primeros capítulos de este fanfic, simplemente con otro título. No voy a dar nombres ni mencionar la plataforma ni a la persona que lo ha hecho, porque creo sinceramente que se trata de alguien joven, que tal vez no entiende la gravedad de sus acciones. No quiero que esa persona reciba una avalancha de odio.

 

Pero, desde aquí, quiero mandarte un mensaje: por favor, detente y borra esa historia. Este fanfic es algo en lo que pongo todo mi cariño, dedicación y esfuerzo. Estoy segura de que tú también tienes el potencial para crear historias maravillosas por tu cuenta, y la satisfacción que sentirás al hacerlo será incomparable. 

 

Si decides continuar con lo que estás haciendo, me veré obligada a tomar medidas, y no quiero llegar al punto de tener que hacer una denuncia pública por plagio o, peor aún, borrar mi propio fanfic.

 

Gracias por leer hasta aquí. Ahora sí, ¡pueden disfrutar del capítulo!

 

 

 

Mk estaba empezando a hartarse de la gente.  

 

No es que no apreciara los cuidados que recibía, por supuesto que no. Su cuerpo estaba más fuerte, sus heridas sanaban con rapidez y, por primera vez en su vida, tenía el estómago lleno todos los días. En apenas cinco días en el palacio, había ganado peso y recuperado algo de color en su rostro. Pero esa sensación de bienestar físico no lograba apagar el torbellino de pensamientos que lo carcomían por dentro.  

 

Su vida había caído en una especie de rutina. Por las mañanas, justo después del desayuno, le cambiaban las vendas y revisaban sus heridas. Luego, los gobernantes se reunieron con los consejeros para revisar asuntos del reino. Si había audiencias, lo dejaban con el Sr. Tang, siempre bajo la atenta vigilancia de los guardias. Al mediodía, casi siempre comían en el jardín, rodeados de pequeños monos que, con chillidos alegres, les robaban la comida cuando bajaban la guardia.  

 

Las tardes estaban reservadas para exploraciones y juegos. Los gobernantes lo llevaban a caminar por la montaña, mostrándole paisajes hermosos que jamás habría imaginado. A veces, jugaban con los pequeños primates, quienes insistían en separarlos en equipos distintos, pues juntos eran prácticamente impares. A Wukong y Macaque no parecía molestarles la competencia entre ellos; de hecho, la disfrutaban con sonrisas desafiantes y miradas llenas de complicidad.  

 

Últimamente, Macaque le había estado enseñando a jugar al Mahjong. El guerrero parecía disfrutarlo de una manera especial, como si jugar con Mk tuviera un significado más profundo para él. Mk, por su parte, se encontraba en las fichas y en la estrategia una distracción que le ayudaba a olvidar, aunque fuera por un momento, el peso de su nueva vida.  

 

Pero la constante atención lo asfixiaba.  

 

Siempre había alguien a su alrededor: guardias con expresiones impenetrables, sirvientes que atendían cualquier necesidad antes incluso de que pudiera expresarla, y sobre todo, los gobernantes, que parecían no querer apartarse de su lado. Dondequiera que girara la cabeza, ahí estaban. Velando por él. Observándolo.  

 

Era… demasiado.  

 

Las únicas veces que lo dejaban con el Sr. Tang —y un pequeño ejército de guardias apostados en las sombras— era cuando Wukong y Macaque asistían a audiencias. Pero incluso entonces, la sensación de estar bajo su vigilancia no desaparecía.  

 

Era sofocante.  

 

Él estaba acostumbrado a la soledad, al silencio, a perderse en sus propios pensamientos sin interrupciones. Ahora, no podía dar un solo paso sin que alguien lo siguiera de cerca.  

 

Necesitaba un respiro. Solo cinco minutos. Sin miradas inquisitivas. Sin voces preocupadas.  

 

Podía cuidarse solo, maldita sea. Lo había hecho toda su vida.  

 

 

Era una mañana soleada, y los gobernantes lo habían dejado una vez más con el Sr. Tang mientras asistían a una reunión sobre asuntos fronterizos. El monje, como de costumbre, estaba sumido en su mundo de tinta y pergaminos, escribiendo con una calma meticulosa que contrastaba con la impaciencia que crecía dentro de Mk.  

 

Era su oportunidad.  

 

Dejó con cuidado los lápices de colores sobre la mesa y se levantó con aparente calma.

 

—Voy al baño —anunció sin mirar directamente al monje.  

 

—Está bien —respondió Tang sin alzar la vista, su voz tranquila, distraída.  

 

Mk salió de la biblioteca con una tranquilidad finga, sintiendo de inmediato la silenciosa presencia de los dos guardias que, como sombras disciplinadas, lo seguían a unos pasos de distancia.  

 

No podía apresurarse. Tenía que parecer casual. Inofensivo.  

 

Sus ojos se posaron en la curva que hacía el pasillo a pocos metros. Sabía exactamente lo que tenía que hacer: ya había memorizado ese rincón, ensayado mentalmente cada movimiento. Solo necesitaba llegar allí.  

 

Apretó el paso apenas un poco, lo suficiente para que no levantara sospechas. Echó un vistazo por encima del hombro. Los guardias mantenían su distancia. Perfecto.  

 

Cinco pasos.  

 

Cuatro.  

 

Tres.  

 

Su cola se tensó con anticipación, como si también supiera que era el momento.  

 

Giró la esquina y, en un solo impulso, saltó sobre una pequeña mesa decorativa que se apoyaba contra la pared. Usó su impulso para impulsarse hacia arriba, aferrándose con manos y pies al gran estandarte que colgaba con orgullo del techo, estampado con el símbolo del reino. Escaló con agilidad, el estandarte ondeando ligeramente bajo su peso. En segundos, se encaramó a las vigas de madera que cruzaban el techo, donde se escondió entre las sombras, conteniendo la respiración.

 

Desde su escondite, observó cómo los dos guardias doblaban la esquina… y se congelaban.  

 

— ¿Dónde está? —susurró uno, ya entrando en pánico.  

 

—¡Lo viste girar por aquí!? —preguntó el otro, con la mirada desorbitada, buscando a su alrededor.  

 

Un segundo después, ambos salieron corriendo en direcciones opuestas, llamándolo a gritos.  

 

Mk soltó al fin el aire contenido en sus pulmones y se permitió una sonrisa orgullosa.  

 

Victoria.

 

 

De un salto preciso, alcanzó la siguiente viga del pasillo, y luego la siguiente… y otra más. Se movía como si el aire mismo lo impulsara, con una ligereza que sólo alguien que había aprendido a sobrevivir en los espacios más estrechos que podía encontrar. En un abrir y cerrar de ojos, encontró una ventana abierta y se deslizó por ella al exterior.  

 

El aire fresco le golpeó el rostro con una mezcla de libertad y adrenalina. Corrió por los senderos de tierra apisonada que rodeaban el castillo, con el corazón latiendo con fuerza y una sonrisa descontrolada curvándole los labios. El viento agitaba su pelaje mientras sus pies se movían con agilidad por un camino que conocía bien.  

 

Finalmente llegó a su un árbol frondoso, de ramas gruesas y firmes, que se alzaba en una colina discreta al borde del jardín oriental. Lo había visto antes desde la distancia, memorizando cada rama como si fuera un mapa secreto. Trepó con destreza, sus garras aferrándose a la corteza, y en pocos segundos se acomodó en una de las ramas más altas.  

 

Con un largo gemido de satisfacción, se estiró como un gato al sol, dejando que su cuerpo descansara al fin. Cerró los ojos y se dejó envolver por el murmullo de las hojas mecidas por el viento, por el calor tibio del sol que se colaba entre el follaje.  

 

Suspiró con alivio. Por fin. Por fin un momento solo. Sin voces, sin manos intentando ayudar, sin ojos encima de él.  

 

La atención constante de los últimos días lo estaba volviendo loco. Agradecía los cuidados, claro, pero no estaba acostumbrado a ellos. Había vivido tanto tiempo escondiéndose del mundo que, ahora, sentirse visto en cada segundo era como vivir bajo una lupa. Esto —este rincón alto, escondido y silencioso— era justo lo que necesitaba.  

 

Volvería antes de que alguien se preocupara de verdad por su ausencia. A tiempo para la comida, con la energía renovada.  

 

Abrió los ojos y los paseó por el horizonte. Desde allí tenía una vista envidiable de la montaña. Podía ver los caminos exteriores que cruzaban entre árboles y terrazas, los puntos brillantes de las armaduras de los soldados que patrullaban los senderos, la majestuosa curva del castillo abrazando el risco.  

 

Y entonces su mirada descendió.  

 

Allí, al pie de la montaña, pegada a la base del castillo, distinguió una puerta de hierro pesado encastrada en la roca. Tres parejas de guerreros la custodiaban, firmes, con espadas desenvainadas que brillaban al sol como advertencias silenciosas.

 

 

 

Debían ser las mazmorras.

 

Mk ladeó la cabeza con curiosidad, las orejas girando con atención. Seis guardias custodiando una sola puerta. Era mucho, incluso para las mazmorras de un palacio como ese.  

 

Uno de los soldados se adelantó, tomó la ancha manilla de hierro y la giró con esfuerzo. El chirrido que emitió la puerta al abrirse fue tan agudo y penetrante que alcanzó hasta la copa del árbol donde estaba Mk, haciéndole fruncir el ceño y echar hacia atrás las orejas con una mueca de incomodidad.  

 

Más allá del umbral, no se veía nada. Solo una negrura espesa, casi viva, que parecía devorar la luz que intentaba colarse dentro. Unas escaleras descendían hacia las profundidades de la montaña, sumidas en una oscuridad que no tenía fondo. El guardia desapareció por ellas sin titubear, tragado por la sombra, y al cabo de unos segundos la puerta volvió a cerrarse tras él con un estruendo sordo que retumbó incluso a esa distancia.  

 

Mk se inclinó hacia delante, apoyando los codos sobre sus rodillas, intrigado. Desde que su vida se había llenado de calma y comodidad, algo nuevo había empezado a crecer dentro de él: una chispa de curiosidad, casi temeraria.  

 

¿Qué habría allí abajo? ¿Serían tan profundas como las minas bajo el orfanato? ¿Más oscuras incluso?  

 

Al pensarlo, un escalofrío le recorrió la columna. Su expresión se endureció y retrocedió un poco sobre la rama, cruzando los brazos. No. Mejor no. Algunas puertas no merecían ser abiertas, ni siquiera con los ojos.  

 

Fue entonces cuando algo más atrajo su atención.  

 

Desde su posición en lo alto, alcanzaba a ver parte del interior del castillo a través de las amplias ventanas y balcones. Y lo que vio hizo que se le tensara el cuerpo. Patrullas de soldados corrían de un lado a otro, como rayas de color cruzando velozmente los pasillos. Se oían gritos, órdenes cortas lanzadas con urgencia. Algunos de los guardias salieron al exterior, armados, formando líneas bajo los estandartes dorados del reino.  

 

Mk se irguió en la rama, inquieto. Su cola se agitó nerviosa a su espalda.  

 

—¿Qué... qué está pasando? —murmuró para sí.  

 

¿Un ataque? No, eso era imposible. Nadie en su sano juicio se atrevería a atacar a los gobernantes del reino, y menos en su propia montaña. Pero el movimiento frenético era real. Se respiraba tensión en el aire como una electricidad que lo erizaba todo.  

 

El cachorro tragó saliva, empezando a sentir cómo una pequeña presión se formaba en su pecho. Ya no se sentía a salvo entre las ramas. Ya no era emocionante.  

 

Decidió que era mejor volver. Cuanto antes.

 

Mk bajó del árbol con la misma agilidad instintiva con la que había trepado minutos antes. Sus patas se deslizaban entre ramas y hojas como si fueran parte de su cuerpo, como si perteneciera a ese lugar elevado. Cada movimiento fluía con la precisión de alguien que había pasado toda su vida huyendo, escondiéndose, sobreviviendo.  

 

Cuando sus pies tocaron el suelo, su respiración se estabilizó, y un leve destello de orgullo cruzó su rostro. Se incorporó de un salto, sacudió las hojas de su túnica, y echó a correr por el sendero de tierra que bordeaba los muros exteriores del castillo.  

 

Pero no llegó muy lejos.  

 

Las sombras del bosque se estremecieron. Fue tan sutil al principio que apenas lo notó: un cambio en la densidad del aire, un murmullo entre los árboles. Luego, todo ocurrió en un segundo.  

 

Las sombras que se proyectaban sobre el suelo comenzaron a moverse. Se deslizaron como tinta derramada, vivas y conscientes, arrastrándose por la tierra en dirección a él.  

 

Mk apenas alcanzó a dar un paso atrás antes de que una oleada de oscuridad le cortara el paso. Tropezó por la sorpresa y cayó de bruces, golpeando el suelo con fuerza. Se incorporó con torpeza, la respiración desbocada, los latidos atronándole en los oídos.  

 

Frente a él, las sombras se alzaron.  

 

Tomaron forma lentamente, como humo que se condensa y se endurece. Dos ojos brillantes emergieron del centro de esa niebla, cargados de furia y ansiedad. La figura terminó de definirse en cuestión de segundos.

 

El guerrero dejó que las sombras se deslizaran de su cuerpo como agua derramada, cayendo en ondas oscuras hasta formar una silueta más humana, más tangible. Su sombra volvió a su sitio, bajo sus pies, como si nada hubiera pasado. Pero todo en él hablaba de furia contenida.

 

Allí se quedó, erguido e imponente, con los hombros tensos, los puños cerrados y el ceño fruncido en una expresión que no aceptaba excusas.

 

Mk abrió la boca para hablar, pero no tuvo oportunidad.

 

—¡Mk! —la voz de Macaque retumbó como un trueno mientras acortaba la distancia en un parpadeo—. ¿¡Dónde demonios has estado!? ¿¡Qué haces fuera solo!?

 

El cachorro dio un paso atrás, pero no fue lo bastante rápido. Las manos de Macaque ya lo sujetaban por los hombros. No con brusquedad, pero sí con una intensidad que lo dejó sin aliento. Los ojos del gobernante, normalmente tranquilos como un lago oscuro, ardían ahora con una tormenta de emociones: preocupación, ira, pánico.

 

—¡No puedes desaparecer así! —su voz tembló, no de debilidad, sino de la tensión de haber contenido el miedo durante demasiado tiempo—. ¡Te hemos estado buscando por todas partes! ¡Creímos que te habían...! —se detuvo, tragando saliva con fuerza.

 

Mk se quedó paralizado, incapaz de hablar. Su corazón latía con tanta fuerza que dolía.

—P-pero... —balbuceó, confundido—. No he estado fuera más de... ¿treinta minutos? 

 

—Jamás vuelvas a salir sin permiso —interrumpió  Macaque con firmeza. Su mirada era dura, inamovible, cargada de una intensidad que no dejaba espacio a protestas—. ¿Me has oído?

 

Mk asintió en silencio, sintiendo cómo las palabras del guerrero se le clavaban en el pecho.

 

Macaque cerró los ojos por un segundo, como si necesitara recomponerse. Luego, sin previo aviso, lo envolvió en un abrazo. Uno de esos abrazos que no solo envolvían el cuerpo, sino también el alma.

 

Mk se quedó quieto al principio. Pero luego, lentamente, permitió que sus manos se aferraran a la tela de la túnica del gobernante. Sintió que los ojos se le llenaban de lágrimas, calientes e inevitables, cargadas con el peso de la culpa, del miedo... y de algo más. Un dolor antiguo y mal enterrado.

 

Cuando Macaque lo condujo de regreso al interior del castillo, lo hizo en silencio. No le soltó la mano ni una sola vez.  

 

Mk mantuvo la cabeza baja, los pasos pequeños, contenidos. No dijo una palabra. Sabía que había causado un problema. Que había enfadado a los gobernantes. Y, por primera vez, eso le dolía más de lo que esperaba.

 

 

Mk mantenía la cabeza baja, los pasos pequeños, casi temerosos. No se atrevía a decir nada. Sentía el peso del silencio más que cualquier grito. Sabía que había causado un problema. Había preocupado a los gobernantes. Pero lo que más le dolía era esa sensación punzante en el pecho: no quería haberlos decepcionado.

 

—Estás castigado —dijo Macaque de repente, su voz seca como un chasquido.

 

Mk levantó la vista, sorprendido. Lo miró con ojos grandes, pero el guerrero no le devolvió la mirada. Seguía caminando, serio, firme, con la vista al frente.

 

—No habrá más paseos por la montaña por un tiempo.

 

Mk sintió que algo se apretaba en su interior.

 

Cruzaron el umbral del castillo. Las puertas se cerraron tras ellos con un estruendo sordo y pesado, seguido por el inconfundible sonido de un cerrojo corriéndose. Un eco metálico que selló más que una entrada.

—Wukong, please listen to me!

—No! It wasn’t supposed to happen like this!

The King's roar echoed through the throne room like thunder. Wukong paced back and forth, his steps resounding with barely contained fury, his hands clenching and unclenching as if he couldn’t decide whether to smash something or hold himself together. Mr. Tang, outwardly calm but deeply worried, watched him cautiously, not daring to interrupt yet.

—He wasn’t supposed to leave! He shouldn’t even have been able to escape! There are guards, there are magic barriers, there’s bloody security! And yet… he’s gone! —Wukong shouted, his voice cracking slightly at the end, caught between rage and fear.

—He’s just a child... —the monk tried gently—. He doesn’t understand the seriousness of what he’s done. He just wanted a moment of peace. He didn’t even stray far from the mountain.

—That doesn’t matter! —Wukong interrupted, his eyes blazing—. It doesn’t matter whether he took one step or a thousand! What matters is that we thought… we thought he had been taken from us again!

An icy silence fell over the room. Macaque, sitting on the throne steps, slowly lifted his head to look at him. Mr. Tang stood frozen, mouth slightly open at the brutal honesty the king had just unleashed.

Wukong took a deep breath, trying to regain control. He walked over to one of the columns and pressed his forehead against it. The cold stone offered no comfort, but it helped him stay grounded.

—The day they took him... we didn’t even know —he murmured in a rough voice, barely able to mask the pain—. Someone entered our room. Our home. And took him away as if it was nothing.

Macaque closed his eyes, his jaw tight. His hands clenched on his knees as he breathed deeply.

—We couldn’t do anything. We didn’t even have time to fight for him —Wukong continued, letting his arms fall limply at his sides—. And now... after everything, after getting him back, seeing him alive, hearing him laugh... thinking for even a second that we had lost him again...

He fell silent, his voice choked by emotions too heavy to name.

Mr. Tang approached slowly, respectfully. He placed a warm, firm hand on Wukong’s shoulder.

—I understand your concern —he said softly—. But Lady Bone Demon has no power anymore. She’s imprisoned. Fragmented.

—I know! —Wukong snapped, turning to him again—. I know! But that doesn’t change the fact that there are still followers out there. Fanatics. Remnants of her madness still waiting for an opportunity. And I’m not risking Xiaotan falling into their hands again. Not ever. I couldn’t survive it.

Silence fell again, this time filled with shared understanding and sorrow. Wukong’s breath came in sharp bursts. Macaque watched him, his eyes dry but heavy with the same fear, the same trauma.

—Wukong —Mr. Tang said serenely—, there will always be danger. There will always be something out there that wants to harm us. But you won’t protect him by locking him inside these walls. All you’ll do is make him feel like you don’t trust him. And that can wound him too.

Wukong looked down, conflicted.

—He doesn’t even know why he’s being punished —the monk added—. He’s too little. You should at least explain it to him.

There was a long pause. Macaque, who had remained silent, finally spoke:

—Exactly... He’s still very small. Small, fragile, and vulnerable. And until LBD is truly destroyed, our cub will not leave this palace. Not again.

His words fell like a sentence, firm and immovable. There was no room for debate.

Wukong approached his husband silently. He took Macaque’s hands in his own, squeezing them gently. Then, with a gesture full of tenderness, he rubbed his cheek against Macaque’s, as if trying to share some of his peace.

—It won’t be long now, my warrior —he whispered with a mix of hope and determination—. They’re searching the mine right now. Sooner or later they’ll find her bones. And when they do, we’ll destroy her for good. This time for real.

Mr. Tang stayed silent, his thoughts turning like gears behind his calm gaze. Finally, he spoke with the careful precision of someone weighing every word:

—Maybe… Mk could benefit from talking to Sandy.

Wukong looked up, thoughtful.

—Sandy...? —he murmured, and after a few seconds, he nodded slowly—. Yes… that might be a good idea. What do you think, Mac?

—Mmm…

—I don’t know anyone more patient and calm than Sandy. Mk could feel safe with him —the monk said, his voice calm but firm.

Macaque didn’t answer immediately. Instead, he summoned a portal of shadows and pulled out a handful of crumpled, torn papers. He handed them silently to the monk.

On them, violent blue lines covered the surface. Erratic, broken strokes. And among them, black silhouettes with empty white eyes, chilling in their rawness.

—And how are you so sure? —Macaque finally asked—. We’ve barely managed to get anything out of him. Not a word about this. He shares almost nothing about what he went through.

Tang looked at the drawings and swallowed hard.

—Because Sandy has a gift. He’s been through a lot himself, and he learned to navigate his emotions without being consumed by them. What Mk needs isn’t another guardian… he needs a safe space where he can start to understand what he feels.

Macaque held his gaze for a long minute. A thick silence settled between them. The warrior searched for any doubt in the monk’s certainty… but found none.

And that was what convinced him.

—Fine —he agreed at last—. When he returns with the ship, tell him everything.

Sandy was much more than just a messenger. Sending him meant complete trust. When a mission was too delicate or important for the common soldiers, the rulers turned to their closest friends. And Sandy was undoubtedly one of them. Even so, Macaque couldn’t help a sliver of distrust. But that... well, that was just his nature.

—Don’t make me regret my decision —he warned, still wary.

Tang nodded firmly.

—...And when do you plan on telling Mk the truth?

The question fell like a stone in the room. Wukong and Macaque looked at each other slowly, as if every second of silence was a conversation between them.

—We can’t postpone it much longer —Wukong finally said, his voice low—. The other kingdoms are already talking. Rumors are spreading like wildfire. And Bull King... —he ran a hand through his hair, exhausted—... he’s about to burst through the door if we keep delaying his visit.

He paused heavily before continuing:

—It’s only been two days, but...

—The longer we wait, the worse he might take it —Macaque finished gravely.

—And worse still if someone else tells him first —Wukong added, like a final verdict.

They all nodded. They knew. They feared it.

The king’s hands trembled slightly. He wanted, with all his heart, for his son to recognize him. To call him "father" without fear. He wanted to tell him how much he had missed him, how much he loved him. He wanted to explain that his anger, his desperation at not finding him, was just the reflection of a visceral terror of losing him again.

But he knew it wouldn’t be that easy.

There might not be immediate hugs. Or sweet words. There might be silence, rejection. Maybe even denial.

—If you’re going to tell him —the monk warned softly—, do it gently. Carefully. Don’t try to convince him in the first try. If he shuts down, let him. Give him time to process, to breathe. And when he’s ready… explain everything. Calmly.

The silence returned, but this time it wasn’t tense. It was more like a pause for acceptance. For preparation. As if everyone in that throne room understood that what was coming was inevitable.

 

 

 

Mk curled up deeper into the blankets, sinking into their warmth as if he could disappear inside them. He slowly chewed a piece of peach, the sweet flavor barely registering on his tongue. He didn’t want to think he was locked up... but technically, he was. There were no visible locks, no bars, but the message had been clear: he couldn’t leave.

After the heavy castle door had closed behind him, Macaque had immediately led him through the corridors without an extra word, his steps long and firm. Along the way they had run into Wukong, who came running from the other side of the palace, his face twisted and his eyes wide open, as if fear still hadn’t left his body.

Mk didn’t know what he said. Everything sounded distant, muffled, like the world was submerged underwater. There was a dull buzzing in his ears that kept him separated from reality. He couldn’t think clearly. His body moved only by inertia, obeying, letting himself be dragged to the royal chamber — the warm nest of blankets, cushions, and soft curtains the rulers used as both bedroom and refuge.

And that’s where he was now. Buried under the duvets, with a bowl of fruit in front of him. The peach between his fingers. The juice slipping down his hand without him noticing. The rulers had left a while ago. They had said something before leaving, he thought, but the words had dissolved before reaching his mind. He only understood that he had to stay there. That he had to eat something. They were always obsessed with him eating.

Mk closed his eyes for a moment, letting the silence wrap around him. It was warm there, safe... and yet, he couldn’t ignore that stabbing feeling in his chest. That jab of sadness coming from a place he couldn’t name. He hadn’t wanted to worry them. He hadn’t wanted to do anything wrong. He just needed some air. He had only wanted to look at the sky for a while.

Yet now he felt more trapped than ever. He was being punished. Isolated. He couldn’t leave. How long would it last? Days? Weeks? Months? Years? A part of his childish, dramatic mind wondered if the rulers would leave him there for centuries. He didn’t know how long gods lived, nor how long he himself lived, but suddenly the idea of never seeing the mountain or the sky again felt unbearably real.

His chest tightened. He had made a mistake... and maybe it was unforgivable.

His line of thought was cut short when the door creaked with a soft click.

Someone had entered.

Mk blinked, disoriented. He hadn’t seen anyone else besides the rulers and himself enter this wing of the palace. The servants never came in, not even to clean. Sun Wukong and Macaque reserved this wing for their total privacy and the door was sealed with magic. Mk wondered if someone had been sent to watch him in case he tried to escape again.

The stranger moved calmly through the room while the cub watched silently from under the blankets. He went here and there, picking up papers from the floor and wiping down surfaces with a cloth. He hummed a song quietly, but it was almost unsettling. Something wasn’t right — the man moved in a mechanical, unnatural way. Mk had the strange feeling he had seen him before.

He hadn’t looked his way yet, but when he turned and their eyes met, Mk could see the paleness and emptiness in his wide pupils. His eyes were completely white.

-Oh! My apologies, I hadn’t seen you, young prince.- he greeted with an exaggerated bow. His mouth was a row of white, far too perfect teeth - We all celebrate your return with joy.

-..What?-
